# neatHack: partner tools, judging, and evidence playbook (locke)

Researched 2026-10-10 against the official pages: neatlogs.com/hackathon, docs.entire.io, github.com/entireio, docs.cfo.ai, docs.neatlogs.com, docs.crustdata.com, and docs.dodopayments.com.
Items marked **[unverified]** were not confirmed in official docs. Check them live with `--help` or on Discord.

---

## 0. TL;DR decisions

1. **Entire is the Git-level recorder for the *dev loop*.** Install it on day 0 with `entire enable --agent claude-code`. Every commit then carries an `Entire-Checkpoint:` trailer. Push often so the checkpoints reach the remote. Add `entire plugin install graph` and export `entire graph checkpoint <id>` and `entire graph diff` output into `evidence/`.
2. **neatlogs is the runtime recorder for the *product agent*.** Call `neatlogs.init()` before importing the LLM SDK, add `@neatlogs.span(kind=...)` on every tool and step, and tag runs `baseline` / `improved` / `recovery`. The before/after numbers come from neatlogs Analytics plus the trace list.
3. **cfo.ai is only the business plan.** Build a 24-month model with Ari, then share a read-only Page link. The docs describe no PDF or Excel export, so also take screenshots. If the build runs out of time, use the cfo.ai MCP only for this; it is not worth wiring into the agent. Cancel the subscription immediately in Settings → Billing.
4. **One sponsor for bonus points: Crustdata,** and only if the agent's task needs company or people data. It is one REST call and costs nothing (5k free credits). Skip Dodo and AWS unless the agent already needs them. Dodo test-mode checkout is the cheap "monetization" story if you want one.
5. **The 25% "use of tools" score depends on *closing the loop*, not just installing.** Show this sequence: neatlogs Detection flags a failure → Fixes suggests a root cause → you fix it in Claude Code (an Entire checkpoint records the reasoning) → rerun → neatlogs shows the metric delta. Put this in the video in one 45-second segment.

---

## 1. Entire (entire.io)

**What it is.** Entire is a developer platform with an MIT-licensed Go CLI (`github.com/entireio/cli`). It hooks into coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot CLI, Gemini, OpenCode, Pi, Factory Droid, Antigravity, and Amp) and stores every agent session (prompts, transcript, tool calls, token usage) alongside your git commits as **checkpoints**. It also offers Git hosting and regional mirrors, cross-repo search, "Brain", "Dispatches", and cross-agent reviews, but none of those are needed for evidence.

**Checkpoint.** A snapshot of an agent session, created when you or the agent make a git commit.
- The commit gets an `Entire-Checkpoint: <id>` trailer. IDs are 26-character ULIDs, or 12-character hex on the legacy backend.
- Storage (CLI ≥0.10.0): refs at `refs/entire/checkpoints/<shard>/<id>`, outside branch history. Legacy repos use the `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch.
- A **pre-push hook pushes the checkpoint refs when you `git push`**. Checkpoints that never reach the remote are invisible to judges.
- Entire never creates commits on your branch (manual-commit strategy). Secrets are redacted before storage.
- Multiple worktrees and concurrent sessions are tracked separately, which matters because AO uses worktrees.

**entire-graph.** An official plugin (`github.com/entireio/entire-graph`, MIT) that builds a local tree-sitter semantic graph of the repo: symbols, callers and callees, routes, change impact. It makes no network or model calls. It is invoked as `entire graph …`. Entire claims up to 71% token savings for agents (self-reported). It can analyze the commit behind a checkpoint, and that is the "entire-graph output" judges ask for.

### Exact commands

```bash
# Install (pick one)
irm https://entire.io/install.ps1 | iex                    # Windows PowerShell
curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash             # macOS/Linux
brew install --cask entireio/tap/entire                    # Homebrew
scoop bucket add entire https://github.com/entireio/scoop-bucket.git; scoop install entire/entire

# Enable in the repo (installs git hooks + agent hooks into .claude/settings.json)
cd Locke
entire enable --agent claude-code          # non-interactive
entire agent add codex                     # optional: if teammates use Codex (.codex/hooks.json) / cursor (.cursor/hooks.json)
entire status                              # shows the sync remote and how many checkpoints are not yet pushed
entire doctor                              # if anything looks off

# Optional: import the last 30 days of Claude Code transcripts as read-only checkpoints
entire import --help                       # [unverified flags] check before use

# Inspect checkpoints
entire checkpoint list                     # current branch; --json for machine output
entire checkpoint explain <id>             # human-readable: prompt, reasoning, files
entire checkpoint explain <id> --generate  # AI summary (needs Claude CLI authed)
entire checkpoint explain <id> --json > evidence/entire/cp-<id>.json
entire checkpoint tokens <id> --compare <baseline-id>   # token usage delta between two checkpoints  ← before/after for free
git for-each-ref refs/entire/checkpoints/  # raw proof
git ls-remote origin 'refs/entire/checkpoints/*'        # proof they reached GitHub
entire recap --week --static               # plain-text recap of agent activity
entire why <file>:<line>                   # "why does this line exist?" (labs/experimental)

# entire-graph
entire plugin install graph
entire graph version
entire graph init-agents --repo .          # writes .entire/agent-guide.md + managed block in AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md
entire graph health --repo . --json > evidence/entire/graph-health.json
entire graph checkpoint <checkpoint-id>    > evidence/entire/graph-cp-<id>.txt   # entity-level changes of that checkpoint's commit
entire graph diff --base <before-sha> --head <after-sha> > evidence/entire/graph-diff.txt
entire graph impact --repo . --symbol <AgentLoop.run>   # blast radius of the recovery change
entire graph snapshot --repo . --format ndjson > evidence/entire/graph.ndjson
```

**Web view (best for the video and README).** `https://entire.io/gh/<org>/<repo>/commit/<sha>` opens the checkpoint's **Sessions** tab (prompt, transcript, tools) and **Changes** tab. You need to log in to entire.io and probably install the Entire GitHub App (`docs.entire.io/guides/repositories/github-app-access.md`). **[unverified]** whether judges can view it without an account. To be safe, also commit `explain --json` dumps.

**Gotchas.**
- Install `entire enable` **before** the first real commit of the hackathon so every commit is checkpointed.
- AO worktrees already have a `.claude/settings.json`. `entire enable --local` writes to `.entire/settings.local.json` if you don't want shared config churn. Entire preserves unrelated Claude settings.
- Read-only *foreground* subagents leave no record. Only subagents launched with `run_in_background` are captured.
- The **product agent's** runtime sessions are not Entire checkpoints unless the agent itself commits via a supported harness. Entire is for the build loop, and neatlogs is for runtime. If locke's agent *is* a coding agent that commits (for example, fixing GitHub issues via Claude Code or Codex), Entire captures the product runs too. That is a strong story: "every agent fix ships with its reasoning attached."

---

## 2. cfo.ai (Ari)

**What it is.** cfo.ai, formerly Runway Financial, sells an "AI CFO" agent named **Ari**. Ari builds a live financial **Model** from questions, connected data (Stripe, Rippling, QuickBooks, Sheets, and others), or an imported spreadsheet. Its main concepts:
- **Scenarios** (what-if branches of the Main model)
- **Pages** (dashboards made of Table and Chart blocks)
- An **MCP server** at `https://api.cfo.ai/mcp`

**Hackathon signup.** Go to `cfo.ai/neathacks`. The neatHack team provides credits, but signup needs a card. Paid plans start with a 14-day trial at $0 today. **Cancel right away in Settings → Billing → Cancel subscription.** Access continues to the end of the trial, and the data persists.

**No export documented.** The docs cover only **sharing a Page as a read-only external link** that needs no login and can be password-protected. There is no PDF, XLSX, or Sheets export in the docs **[unverified: check the Page menu in-app]**. Plan to submit the share link, screenshots of each Page, and a markdown summary committed to `docs/business-plan.md`.

### Exact steps (~45 minutes)

1. Sign up at `cfo.ai/neathacks` → start the trial → **cancel immediately** in Settings → Billing.
2. Open a chat with Ari and paste the prompts below in order. They follow the official "build from scratch" guidance.
   - "We are a pre-revenue startup with no historical data. Build a 24-month monthly model with editable assumptions, every input labeled as assumed."
   - "Pricing: three plans — Free, Pro at $X/mo, Team at $Y/seat/mo. Revenue = customers × average price. Add annual-plan discount."
   - "Growth: N new signups/month growing G%, free→paid conversion C%, monthly churn K%."
   - "Costs: LLM inference cost per agent run = $Z (from our neatlogs traces) × runs per customer; hosting $H/mo; two founders at $S salary starting month 4; marketing $M/mo."
   - "Customers pay upfront monthly via Dodo Payments with 4% + 40¢ fees; model cash timing."
   - "Starting cash $C0. Show ending cash by month and runway in months as a visible formula (ending cash ÷ avg monthly net burn)."
   - "Create Scenarios: 'Price +20%' and 'LLM cost −50% (after caching fix)'; compare runway and ending cash to Main."
   - "Build a Page summarizing pricing, unit economics (gross margin per run), revenue, burn, runway, and the scenario comparison."
3. Open the Page → **Share** → choose the Scenario → **External access → Create link** → **Copy external link**. Leave the password off so judges can open it.
4. Screenshot each block into `evidence/cfo/` and write a one-page summary in `docs/business-plan.md` with the link.

**Killer move for the 25% bucket.** Feed **real per-run cost from neatlogs** (the trace cost column) into the cfo.ai unit-economics assumption. Then show that the agent improvement (fewer tokens or retries) moves gross margin and runway in the "LLM cost −50%" scenario. That one sentence connects all three mandatory tools.

**Optional MCP** (Starter plan or higher; works during the trial): `claude mcp add --transport http cfoai https://api.cfo.ai/mcp`, then `/mcp` → cfoai → Authenticate. Tools include `inspect_pages`, `edit_pages`, `inspect_scenarios`, `edit_scenarios`, `edit_table_blocks`, and `list_orgs`. Use it to let Claude Code push updated cost numbers into the scenario. A nice demo beat, but optional.

---

## 3. neatlogs: what to use to impress neatlogs judges

**Product.** neatlogs is observability for AI agents. It traces runs, flags failures, and tracks fixes. Features at docs.neatlogs.com:

| Feature | What it gives you | Judge value |
|---|---|---|
| **Traces** | span tree and timeline with cost, latency, and token columns (prompt, completion, cache hits, TTFT) | baseline vs improved numbers |
| **Session Replay** (experimental) | step-by-step playback, structure graph, Story and Tree views | ★ great 10-second video beat |
| **Detections** | rules (regex, condition, PII, classifier) that badge failing spans live | ★ shows the failure in the recovery run |
| **Fixes (triage)** | AI root-cause suggestions from flagged traces: code location and recommended change. Can dispatch to Cursor Cloud Agents. Mark as deployed. MCP tools `triage_list`, `triage_get`, `triage_accept` | ★★ "neatlogs told us what to fix" (the loop they built the product for) |
| **Investigate** (AI search) | natural-language queries over traces | nice-to-have |
| **Analytics** | aggregate cost, latency, errors, and detection trends | ★ before/after chart |
| **Experiments** | versioned **Prompts** with labels (`production`/`staging`) and a Playground. Datasets are "coming soon" | prompt v1 → v2 as the "improvement" with label rollback |
| **Alerts**, **Comments** | team annotations | minor |
| **Tools & MCPs** | per-tool and per-MCP-call analytics | good if the agent is tool-heavy |

### Exact setup (Python)

```bash
pip install -U "neatlogs[anthropic]"      # or [openai]; Python >=3.10,<3.14
export NEATLOGS_API_KEY=...               # from app.neatlogs.com; without it spans are NOT exported
# or guided: npx @neatlogs/wizard
```
```python
import os, neatlogs
neatlogs.init(api_key=os.environ["NEATLOGS_API_KEY"], workflow_name="locke",
              instrumentations=["anthropic"], tags=["baseline"])   # MUST run before importing anthropic
import anthropic

@neatlogs.span(kind="TOOL", tool_name="run_tests")      # kinds: WORKFLOW AGENT CHAIN TOOL RETRIEVER EMBEDDING GUARDRAIL MCP_TOOL
def run_tests(...): ...

with neatlogs.trace("plan", kind="AGENT") as span:
    span.set_attribute("locke.step", "plan")
...
neatlogs.flush(); neatlogs.shutdown()     # end of script, or the last spans are lost
```
- LangGraph and LangChain: use `neatlogs.langchain_handler()`, not an instrumentation key.
- **Claude Agent SDK is not in the supported list.** Use the `anthropic` instrumentation plus manual `@span`, or the `mcp` instrumentation.
- TypeScript: explicit wrappers and handlers. See `/sdk/typescript`.
- `neatlogs.identify(...)` sets session and user. See `/sdk/sessions`.

**CLI for evidence** (Node 22 or 24): `npm i -g neatlogs-cli@0.2.0` → `neatlogs auth login` → `neatlogs traces list --json`, `neatlogs traces get <id> --json > evidence/neatlogs/<id>.json`. Public trace sharing is **[unverified]**. The CLI has `neatlogs sharing` and `neatlogs guest-links mint --evaluation <id> --recipient-email <e>`, which is email-scoped. Plan on **screenshots plus exported JSON plus the dashboard URL**, and ask in Discord whether judges get project access.

**Most impressive to neatlogs judges, in rank order:**
1. The Detection → Fixes → code change → rerun loop, done on camera.
2. Tags `baseline`/`improved` with ≥10 runs each and a numeric table (success rate, avg cost, p50 latency, retries).
3. Session Replay of the recovery run.
4. A custom Detection rule you wrote, for example regex on a `"status":"error"` tool output or a condition on retries > 2.
5. Prompt versioning via Experiments as the "what changed" artifact.

---

## 4. Sponsors: cheap bonus leverage

| Sponsor | Effort | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| **Crustdata** (5k credits per participant) | 1 REST call. `POST https://api.crustdata.com/company/search` (also `/person/search`, enrich, jobs, web search) with headers `authorization: Bearer <key>` and `x-api-version: 2025-11-01` | **Do it only if** locke's task touches companies or people (lead research, due diligence, enrichment). Wrap it as a `@neatlogs.span(kind="TOOL")` so it shows in traces. Its 4xx and rate limits make a natural **recovery-run failure**. |
| **Dodo Payments** (credits are the prize, so judges like it) | Test mode is about 15 minutes. `claude plugins marketplace add dodopayments/dodo-agent-plugin && claude plugins install dodopayments@dodopayments`. Or use a dashboard **payment link** with no code. Has usage-based and credit billing for per-run agent pricing. | **Cheap story:** a dashboard payment link in the README with the cfo.ai pricing tiers matching. Do a real API integration only if there's spare time on day 2. |
| **AWS** ($25, us-east-1, EC2, Lambda, IAM, ALB; no Bedrock) | 1–3 hours | Do it only if the agent must "watch a running system" or needs a public endpoint. A Lambda or a t3.small hosting the demo is enough. Not judged directly. |
| **Orchestrator.inc** (judge's company) | n/a | Multi-agent coordination with visible handoffs in traces will resonate. Don't name-drop. |

---

## 5. What wins: patterns and a demo-video recipe

**Patterns that score on trace, recovery, and verification rubrics:**
- **Narrow task, end-to-end, with a verifiable oracle.** Pick a task where success is machine-checkable (tests pass, answer matches sources, a URL returns 200). Judges trust numbers they can recompute.
- **Explicit plan → act → verify → repair loop** with each phase as a named span (`AGENT plan`, `TOOL x`, `GUARDRAIL verify`, `AGENT repair`). The trace tree should *read like the architecture diagram*.
- **Designed-in failure.** Inject a real failure (a flaky tool, a rate limit, a wrong file path, a schema change). Show detection → retry with changed strategy → verified success. Do not hide errors. The rubric explicitly asks for them.
- **Measured improvement.** Fix a fixed eval set of 10–20 tasks, then run it with the v1 baseline and the v2 improved version. Report success rate, cost per task, latency, tool errors, and retries. One table, one chart.
- **Provenance.** Every claim in the README links to a trace, a checkpoint, or a commit.
- **Build in public with substance.** Posts with screenshots of traces and numbers beat "day 1 vibes."

**Demo video (20%, aim for 2:30–3:00):**

| t | Beat |
|---|---|
| 0:00–0:15 | Problem plus a one-line hook ("locke does X end-to-end while you sleep") |
| 0:15–1:00 | Live end-to-end run, sped up 2–4×, with the neatlogs trace filling in alongside |
| 1:00–1:35 | **Recovery:** failure happens → Detection badge → agent replans → verified success (Session Replay) |
| 1:35–2:05 | **Improvement:** the neatlogs Fixes suggestion → the Entire checkpoint of the fix (entire.io Sessions tab) → before/after table |
| 2:05–2:30 | **Business:** cfo.ai Page showing pricing, unit cost from real traces, and runway, plus the "cost −50%" scenario |
| 2:30–2:50 | Architecture in one slide, repo link, #neatHack |

Rules for the video:
- Captions on, real footage (not slides) for at least 70%.
- Zoom into the numbers.
- No dead air waiting on LLMs. Cut or speed it up.
- Name the three tools out loud while they're on screen.

---

## 6. Evidence checklist mapped to judging weight

Put everything under `evidence/` plus a README section "Evidence" with links.

**The agent (30%)**
- [ ] One-command run (`make demo` / `python -m locke run <task>`) and a README quickstart
- [ ] A fixed eval set (`evals/tasks.jsonl`, 10–20 items) and a scorer script
- [ ] An architecture diagram showing plan, act, verify, and repair with state and context handling
- [ ] **Recovery run:** a trace ID and screenshot where a tool failed and the agent recovered, with a short write-up of what failed, how it was detected, and what it changed
- [ ] Verification step evidence: tests run or sources checked, as a `GUARDRAIL` span

**Use of neatlogs + Entire + cfo.ai (25%)**
- [ ] neatlogs: baseline and improved trace links or screenshots, and an Analytics chart
- [ ] neatlogs: a custom Detection rule plus a Fixes suggestion you acted on (link the commit)
- [ ] neatlogs: `evidence/neatlogs/*.json` exported via the CLI

# Locke tech-stack research

**As verified:** 10 October 2026  
**Constraint:** Next.js App Router + TypeScript, LangGraph, neatlogs (mandatory), OpenRouter for every LLM call.  
**Scope:** research only; no repository changes.

## Decision brief

Use a single TypeScript application: Next.js App Router on the Node runtime, an in-process LangGraph.js graph, OpenRouter through `ChatOpenAI`, and the native `neatlogs` TypeScript SDK. A Python service and a generic OTLP bridge are unnecessary: neatlogs now publishes a Node/TypeScript SDK and a first-party LangChain/LangGraph callback handler.

For the 48-hour build, stream `graph.stream()` events from a Node route with native Web Streams/SSE. Do not introduce a separate LangGraph Agent Server just to use `useStream`; it adds a second runtime and deployment surface. If the product already needs durable hosted threads, then use Agent Server + `@langchain/react` instead.

The principal risk is version compatibility. neatlogs 1.1.21 documents a verified LangChain compatibility baseline of `@langchain/core` 0.3.x, while current LangGraph 1.4.x requires Core 1.x. Use the pinned 0.3-compatible cohort below and prove one persisted trace before building the rest of the UI. Do not casually upgrade LangChain packages during the hackathon.

## 1. neatlogs findings

### Native SDK: TypeScript is supported

This is no longer Python-only. The official [TypeScript SDK documentation](https://docs.neatlogs.com/sdk/typescript) says the npm package is `neatlogs`, supports Node.js 18/20/22, and uses explicit wrappers/handlers rather than Python-style auto-instrumentation. npm currently lists [`neatlogs` 1.1.21](https://www.npmjs.com/package/neatlogs).

Install the verified hackathon pin:

```bash
pnpm add -E neatlogs@1.1.21
```

Minimal server initialization:

```ts
import { init, flush } from "neatlogs";

const neatlogsReady = init({
  apiKey: process.env.NEATLOGS_API_KEY,
  workflowName: "locke-agent",
  tags: ["neathack-2026"],
});
```

`init()` is asynchronous. In a Next route, keep one module-level initialization promise, await it per request, and call `await flush()` after the response stream has fully completed. Do not call `shutdown()` for every request because a warm serverless runtime must remain reusable. The SDK's [lifecycle guidance](https://docs.neatlogs.com/sdk/typescript) explicitly says serverless handlers should flush per invocation and only shut down when the runtime is actually torn down.

Use a Node route, not Edge:

```ts
export const runtime = "nodejs";
```

The npm package states that Edge runtime packaging is unsupported. This is the decisive limitation for Next.js, not App Router itself.

### Exact LangGraph tracing path

Use the callback handler; do not pass `instrumentations: ["langchain"]` in TypeScript.

```ts
import { langchainHandler } from "neatlogs/langchain";

await neatlogsReady;
const handler = langchainHandler();
const stream = await graph.stream(input, {
  configurable: { thread_id: threadId },
  callbacks: [handler],
  streamMode: ["messages", "updates"],
});
```

Attach one handler at the **graph invocation**, not to each node/model call. Reuse that handler for the entire run. The official [LangChain/LangGraph integration guide](https://docs.neatlogs.com/integrations/langchain) says this is what preserves graph node boundaries and nests LLM spans under the right node; a fresh handler per model call splits/orphans spans. The callback captures LLM calls, chains, tools, retrievers, graph node boundaries, tool loops, token usage, inputs/outputs, timings, and errors.

This works in a Next.js App Router route handler as long as it runs in the Node runtime and the stream is fully consumed before flushing. An interrupted/cancelled response must close the graph/model spans before `flush()`; flushing cannot finalize an open span.

### Trace IDs and links

The TypeScript callback API does not document a trace URL as the return value of `graph.invoke()`/`graph.stream()`. Practical paths are:

1. Open the run in the neatlogs **Traces** dashboard; each row is a run and opens its trace.
2. Query it with `neatlogs traces list --json` / `neatlogs traces get '<trace-id>' --json`; the [CLI guide](https://docs.neatlogs.com/cli) documents both.
3. The neatlogs MCP `search_traces` result includes a canonical link of the form `https://neatlogs.com/traces/<trace-id>`; see the [MCP tools reference](https://docs.neatlogs.com/integrations/mcp-tools).
4. For external judges, create a dashboard guest/share link when the project plan permits it. Do not expose an ingest key or service-account token to the browser.

Tag every run with a stable app run ID / scenario ID so it is easy to find. For demo screenshots, save the actual dashboard/share URL after the trace is persisted rather than constructing a URL optimistically.

### Official skill / getting-started resources

- [Agent Skills guide](https://docs.neatlogs.com/integrations/skills): install the TypeScript skill with `npx skills add neatlogs/skills --skill "neatlogs-ts"`.
- [Instrumentation Wizard](https://docs.neatlogs.com/docs/quickstart/wizard): `npx @neatlogs/wizard` detects the stack and installs the applicable SDK/skill.
- [TypeScript SDK quickstart](https://docs.neatlogs.com/sdk/typescript).
- [neatHack page](https://neatlogs.com/hackathon): explicitly requires tracing every agent run and comparing runs to verify fixes.

No separate hackathon-only “Start with neatlogs” SDK page was discoverable in the official site/GitHub results. The official Agent Skills page and Wizard are the current start paths.

### Evals, prompt versions, and numeric improvement

Yes, with one caveat:

- **Evals:** real traces can be sent to human reviewers, AI evaluators, or both, using structured questions; results aggregate into overall, per-question, and recurring-batch metrics and export as CSV/JSON ([Human Evaluators](https://docs.neatlogs.com/docs/features/evals/human-evaluators)).
- **Prompt versioning:** Experiments stores named, labelled prompt versions and supports rollback; the Playground can test a version before promotion ([Experiments](https://docs.neatlogs.com/docs/features/experiments)).
- **Operational comparisons:** Analytics exposes error rate, latency, token usage, cost, tool performance, and detection trends, filterable by workflow/model/tool/detection ([Analytics](https://docs.neatlogs.com/docs/features/analytics)).
- **Caveat:** labelled evaluation **Datasets** are still marked “coming soon.” Do not pitch that as available.

Recommended demo measurement:

| Metric | Before/after method |
|---|---|
| Task success | Same 15-30 fixed cases; binary rubric in a neatlogs eval |
| Verifier score | 1-5 structured AI-evaluator score, spot-checked by a human |
| Tool correctness | Correct tool + valid arguments / eligible tool opportunities |
| Reliability | Trace error rate and failed-tool detection rate |
| Efficiency | Median/p95 latency, tokens, and cost per successful task |

Run the exact same cases with tags such as `variant:baseline` and `variant:improved`, keep model/temperature/provider policy fixed, and report sample size plus absolute values (for example, `11/20 -> 17/20`, not only “+30%”). This yields a defensible “improvement with numbers” story even without the forthcoming Datasets feature. Note the current [evaluation workflow caveat](https://docs.neatlogs.com/cli/release-workflows): short scheduled collections can miss traces arriving after the last matcher pass, so verify the final cohort manually for the hackathon.

## 2. Python-only contingency

Not applicable: the first-party TypeScript SDK and LangGraph callback make the cleanest choice an all-TypeScript Node deployment.

If the handler proves incompatible with the chosen LangChain build, prefer this fallback order:

1. Pin the known `@langchain/core` 0.3-compatible package family below.
2. Add manual neatlogs semantic spans around the graph/model/tool boundaries.
3. Only then use generic OTLP export to the documented `/v1/traces` OTLP endpoint.

Do **not** introduce FastAPI + Python LangGraph solely for tracing. It duplicates graph types, streaming, auth, deployment, and failure handling. A Python service only becomes sensible if the agent already depends on Python-only libraries.

## 3. LangGraph.js + OpenRouter

### `ChatOpenAI` configuration

```ts
import { ChatOpenAI } from "@langchain/openai";

export const workerModel = new ChatOpenAI({
  apiKey: process.env.OPENROUTER_API_KEY,
  model: "openai/gpt-5.6-luna",
  temperature: 0,
  maxRetries: 2,
  configuration: {
    baseURL: "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1",
    defaultHeaders: {
      "HTTP-Referer": process.env.APP_URL ?? "http://localhost:3000",
      "X-OpenRouter-Title": "Locke",
    },
  },
});
```

LangChain's current [`ChatOpenAI` reference](https://reference.langchain.com/javascript/langchain-openai/ChatOpenAI) puts the endpoint under `configuration.baseURL`. OpenRouter's [framework guide](https://openrouter.ai/docs/community/frameworks) confirms the OpenAI-compatible base URL, while [app attribution](https://openrouter.ai/docs/app-attribution) documents `HTTP-Referer` and `X-OpenRouter-Title`. Keep the API key server-side.

### Tools

Define LangChain tools with Zod and bind them with `model.bindTools(tools)`, or use a LangGraph prebuilt tool node. OpenRouter standardizes OpenAI-style function calling, but support is still model-specific. Use model pages/collections that explicitly show `tools` and `tool_choice`; the [tool-calling guide](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/features/tool-calling) explains the request/execute/result loop.

Treat tools as untrusted boundaries: validate arguments, enforce authorization in the tool implementation, make mutations idempotent, return bounded outputs, and never trust the model's claim that a tool succeeded.

### Streaming choice

**Recommended for this 48-hour build:** `graph.stream(..., { streamMode: ["messages", "updates"] })` inside `app/api/agent/route.ts`, convert chunks to a native `ReadableStream`/SSE response, and consume with a small client hook. This keeps the graph, neatlogs handler, and cancellation lifecycle in one Node process.

Alternatives:

- **AI SDK adapter:** `@ai-sdk/langchain` can convert `graph.stream()` into an AI SDK `UIMessageStream` in a Next route; the official [adapter guide](https://ai-sdk.dev/providers/adapters/langchain) supports messages, tools, results, and custom data. It is ergonomically good, but its current 3.x/current-Core dependency lane must be reconciled with neatlogs' verified Core 0.3.x baseline before adoption.
- **`useStream` / LangGraph SDK:** use when there is a LangGraph Agent Server (local or deployed) providing threads/runs. Current React integration is `@langchain/react` v1, whose [README](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraphjs/blob/main/libs/sdk-react/README.md) covers `useStream`. It is unnecessary infrastructure for an in-process Next route.
- **Do not mix generations:** older examples import `useStream` from `@langchain/langgraph-sdk/react`; current v1 moved it to `@langchain/react` and changed protocol/return shapes.

### Checkpointer

- **Local, single-process demo:** `MemorySaver` is the fastest start.
- **Hosted demo, multi-instance Next, or any meaningful interrupt/resume:** use `PostgresSaver` from `@langchain/langgraph-checkpoint-postgres`; npm documents `PostgresSaver.fromConnString(...)` and the required one-time `.setup()` ([package](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@langchain/langgraph-checkpoint-postgres)).

Recommendation: start with `MemorySaver` only for day-one local flow work, then switch to Postgres before deploying if human approval is a judged feature. MemorySaver disappears on restart and can route consecutive requests to different serverless instances, breaking thread continuity.

### Human in the loop

Compile with a checkpointer; use a stable `thread_id`; call `interrupt(payload)` inside the review node; resume the same thread with `new Command({ resume: decision })`. LangGraph's [human-in-the-loop example](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/javascript/langgraph/thinking-in-langgraph) confirms that `interrupt()` persists state and resumes via `Command`. Put `interrupt()` before side effects because code before it may run again on resume.

```ts
const decision = interrupt({ action: "approve", draft });
// Resume later:
await graph.invoke(new Command({ resume: decision }), config);
```

Never place an irreversible action before the approval interrupt. Make the post-approval action idempotent so retries cannot duplicate it.

## 4. OpenRouter model split (10 October 2026)

Prices are OpenRouter's currently listed standard per-million-token rates; promotions and provider routing can change, so re-check before the final demo.

| Role | Recommended slug | Input / output per 1M | Why |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Planner | `openai/gpt-5.6-sol` | $2.00 / $10.00 | Flagship long-horizon reasoning and agentic planning; call once per task, not in every loop. [Model page](https://openrouter.ai/openai/gpt-5.6-sol) |
| Worker | `openai/gpt-5.6-luna` | $0.20 / $1.20 | Cheap, fast tool-use/classification/execution loops; 1.05M context and explicit tool/structured-output support. [Model page](https://openrouter.ai/openai/gpt-5.6-luna) |
| Verifier | `google/gemini-3.8-flash` | $0.75 / $3.75 promotional | Independent model family, 1M context, strong current agentic/coding scores, tool and structured-output support. [Model page](https://openrouter.ai/google/gemini-3.8-flash) |

Use deterministic structured output for planner and verifier. Keep the verifier isolated from the worker's hidden reasoning; give it the task, evidence/tool outputs, final answer, and rubric. Escalate only failed/ambiguous cases to `anthropic/claude-sonnet-4.6` ($3/$15) or `openai/gpt-5.6-sol`, rather than paying frontier rates on every worker step.

## 5. Pins, gotchas, and skeleton

### Proposed compatibility-first pins

These are an **integration cohort to smoke-test**, not a claim that neatlogs officially certifies every exact patch combination:

```text
Node.js                              22.x
next                                16.4.0
neatlogs                            1.1.21
@langchain/core                     0.3.79
@langchain/langgraph                0.4.10
@langchain/openai                   0.6.17
zod                                 3.25.76
```

Why the older LangChain lane: neatlogs 1.1.21 documents `@langchain/core` 0.3.x as its verified baseline, while current [`@langchain/langgraph` 1.4.21](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@langchain/langgraph) peers on Core 1.x. npm still publishes the 0.4.x LangGraph backport line and the 0.6.x OpenAI provider line. Lock the pnpm lockfile and add a package-manager override so exactly one `@langchain/core` is installed.

Before accepting the cohort, run:

1. Typecheck/build.
2. One model call through OpenRouter.
3. One tool call.
4. One graph interrupt/resume.
5. One streamed cancellation.
6. `pnpm exec neatlogs doctor --local --json`, then `--probe --json` with the project key.
7. Open the persisted trace and verify graph node -> LLM/tool nesting, token counts, and final status.

If neatlogs confirms Core 1.x support during the event, prefer the current family (`@langchain/core` 1.2.x, LangGraph 1.4.x, `@langchain/openai` 1.6.x) as a coordinated upgrade—not a piecemeal bump.

### Gotchas

- Next route must be Node runtime; neatlogs TypeScript does not support Edge packaging.
- `init()` and `flush()` must be awaited; do not `shutdown()` each warm serverless invocation.
- Fully consume/end streams before flushing; handle abort signals and error paths.
- Attach one neatlogs handler at graph invocation, not per node.
- A callback trace is not proven until it appears in the dashboard/probe readback.
- Never put `NEATLOGS_API_KEY` or `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` in client code.
- OpenRouter model aliases/prices/providers change. Pin explicit model slugs and record the slug/provider in trace metadata.
- Tool-call reliability varies by model/provider; use OpenRouter's tool-capability pages and test the exact schema.
- Preserve provider-specific reasoning metadata across multi-turn tool calls when the selected model requires it.
- `MemorySaver` is process-local, not serverless-durable.
- `interrupt()` replays the node on resume; avoid pre-interrupt side effects.
- Prompt labels/versions and evaluation variant tags must be captured on every trace to make comparisons auditable.

### Minimal file skeleton

```text
app/
  page.tsx                         # task input, live run, approval UI
  api/agent/route.ts               # Node route; stream start/resume
  api/evals/route.ts               # optional fixed-case harness endpoint
components/
  run-console.tsx                  # messages, node/tool progress, interrupt card
lib/
  env.ts                           # server-only validated env
  models.ts                        # OpenRouter ChatOpenAI instances by role
  neatlogs.ts                      # singleton init promise, handler factory, flush
  agent/
    state.ts                       # typed graph state
    tools.ts                       # validated/idempotent tools
    nodes.ts                       # planner, worker, verifier, approval
    graph.ts                       # graph + checkpointer compile
    stream.ts                      # graph chunks -> SSE/UI events
  evals/
    cases.ts                       # fixed small benchmark cases
    score.ts                       # deterministic + verifier rubric aggregation
scripts/
  run-evals.ts                     # baseline/improved batch runner
.env.example                       # names only; no secrets
```

## Final recommendation

Proceed with native TypeScript neatlogs in a Next Node route and no Python service. Make “first persisted, correctly nested neatlogs trace” the initial technical gate. Use OpenRouter Sol -> Luna -> Gemini Flash for planner/worker/verifier, MemorySaver locally and Postgres for a hosted interrupt demo, and a fixed tagged eval set to show before/after task success, verifier score, latency, tokens, and cost. The single highest-risk item is the neatlogs Core 0.3 compatibility boundary; freeze the proposed cohort until an end-to-end trace proves it.

# Product Use Case & Vision
## AI-Powered Job Opportunity Verification and Safe Application Assistance

**Product category:** Consumer SaaS / Career Safety / AI-Assisted Investigation  
**Primary audience:** Job seekers, students, fresh graduates, remote professionals, and career switchers  
**Secondary audience:** Universities, career centers, recruitment platforms, and employers  
**Core objective:** Help people distinguish legitimate employment opportunities from suspicious recruitment attempts and safely navigate toward authentic hiring channels.

---

# 1. Executive Summary

Finding a job has become increasingly digital, convenient, and accessible. Candidates discover opportunities through job boards, professional networks, company websites, social media, messaging platforms, and unsolicited recruiter outreach.

However, this accessibility has also introduced a significant trust problem.

Fraudulent recruiters can impersonate legitimate companies, replicate genuine job descriptions, create misleading application websites, and approach candidates using convincing messages.

A candidate might be interested in a completely legitimate job opening while unknowingly interacting with an unauthorized person pretending to recruit for it.

Existing solutions often emphasize recognizing suspicious messages, identifying known scam patterns, or providing general safety guidance.

**Our product aims to go beyond identifying potential fraud.**

It will function as an independent job-opportunity investigation assistant that evaluates recruitment claims, establishes what can actually be verified, identifies inconsistencies, and helps candidates find a legitimate route to the employer.

The ultimate objective is not simply to tell users whether something looks suspicious.

It is to help them answer:

> "I received this job opportunity. Can I trust it, what evidence supports it, and how can I safely proceed if the opportunity is genuine?"

The product should reduce uncertainty without making unsupported claims of absolute safety.

---

# 2. Problem Statement

## 2.1 The underlying problem: Candidates cannot easily establish recruitment authenticity

Today's recruitment ecosystem is highly fragmented.

A single job opportunity may involve several independent parties:

- The company advertising a position.
- A hiring manager or HR representative.
- An external recruitment agency.
- A job-listing platform.
- An applicant-tracking or application website.
- Communication through email, LinkedIn, WhatsApp, or other channels.

Candidates are expected to trust these interactions despite having limited visibility into the relationships between the parties.

A professional-looking message, a recognizable company logo, or even a real job description is not sufficient evidence that the sender is authorized to recruit.

### Example

A candidate receives a message offering a remote software engineering position at a well-known company.

The recruiter shares a convincing job description, competitive compensation, and a link to complete the application.

The company exists.

The job title exists.

The description closely matches a publicly advertised vacancy.

However, the recruiter's email belongs to a separate domain, and the supplied application website is not associated with the employer's known hiring channels.

A candidate may struggle to determine whether the recruiter represents an authorized staffing agency, an internal hiring team using another domain, or someone impersonating the company.

**The problem is not necessarily the job itself. It is the authenticity of the recruitment interaction and the route through which the candidate is being asked to proceed.**

## 2.2 Consequences for job seekers

### Financial exposure

Fraudulent recruiters may ask candidates to pay registration fees, onboarding deposits, equipment costs, or other charges under the promise of employment.

### Personal information exposure

Candidates may be asked to disclose sensitive documents, bank details, identity information, or other personal data before establishing that the recruitment process is legitimate.

### Lost time and effort

Candidates can spend days participating in interviews, completing assignments, or communicating with supposed recruiters before discovering that the opportunity was misleading or fraudulent.

### Emotional and professional impact

False employment promises can create anxiety, disappointment, damaged confidence, and disruption to legitimate job-search efforts.

### Missed legitimate opportunities

Suspicious-looking communication is not always fraudulent. Genuine recruiters sometimes work through external agencies, alternative hiring platforms, or unfamiliar communication channels.

An overly aggressive scam detector could discourage someone from pursuing a genuine opportunity.

**Our product must address both risks: proceeding with an unsafe opportunity and unnecessarily abandoning a legitimate one.**

---

# 3. Product Vision

## 3.1 What are we building?

An AI-powered service that independently investigates employment opportunities and provides evidence-backed recommendations for safely proceeding.

Users should be able to submit a job listing, recruiting message, recruiter details, or application link and ask the product to verify the opportunity.

Instead of producing a generic warning, the product will investigate multiple independent questions:

1. Is the organization real and identifiable?
2. Can the advertised vacancy be independently confirmed?
3. Does the recruitment communication appear consistent with the employer's known hiring practices?
4. Is there credible evidence connecting the recruiter to the employer?
5. Does the supplied application destination match a legitimate hiring channel?
6. Are there suspicious or potentially harmful requests?
7. If the communication is unreliable, can the user reach the genuine opportunity through another verified route?

Each question should receive its own evidence-backed finding.

## 3.2 Product mission

**Make employment opportunities easier to verify and safer to pursue, regardless of where a candidate discovers them.**

## 3.3 Long-term vision

Become a trusted verification and navigation layer between job seekers and recruitment channels.

The product should eventually help candidates evaluate opportunities across different platforms without forcing them to change how they search for jobs.

It is not intended to replace job boards, recruitment agencies, or professional networks.

Rather, it should help users independently establish trust before committing their time, money, or sensitive information.

---

# 4. Target Users and Their Needs

## 4.1 Students and fresh graduates

**Situation:** Limited professional experience and unfamiliarity with formal recruitment practices.

**Problems:**
- Difficulty distinguishing legitimate recruiters from impersonators.
- Greater uncertainty about onboarding fees and document requests.
- Limited knowledge of authentic employer hiring channels.
- High exposure to unsolicited employment and internship offers.

**Expected value:** A straightforward way to verify opportunities and understand what actions are safe before sharing sensitive information.

## 4.2 Experienced professionals and career switchers

**Situation:** Actively evaluating opportunities from unfamiliar organizations, recruiters, or recruitment agencies.

**Problems:**
- Uncertainty around external recruitment firms.
- Confusing job links and company domains.
- Difficulty establishing whether a vacancy is current.
- Time spent manually searching company websites and contacting employers.

**Expected value:** Faster, evidence-backed assessments and direct navigation to independently verified hiring channels.

## 4.3 Remote and international job seekers

**Situation:** Considering employment with companies in other countries, often without local contacts.

**Problems:**
- Limited familiarity with foreign employers and recruitment norms.
- Difficulty identifying legitimate overseas hiring arrangements.
- Additional uncertainty around relocation, remote work, visas, and contractual terms.
- Higher practical barriers to independently contacting or visiting employers.

**Expected value:** Independent verification of employment opportunities across geographical boundaries, while making clear which immigration or employment claims remain unverified.

## 4.4 Universities and career centers

**Situation:** Supporting large numbers of students entering the workforce.

**Problems:**
- Students encountering questionable internship and placement offers.
- Career advisers repeatedly performing manual checks.
- Difficulty providing consistent and evidence-based guidance.
- Limited visibility into common risks affecting students.

**Expected value:** A scalable resource for student safety, career guidance, and employment-opportunity verification.

## 4.5 Recruitment platforms and employers

**Situation:** Legitimate recruiters and companies may be impersonated by third parties.

**Problems:**
- Fraudulent parties misusing company names and branding.
- Candidates distrusting legitimate recruitment outreach.
- Reputational damage caused by impersonation.
- Difficulty communicating recognized hiring channels.

**Expected value:** An additional mechanism for making authentic recruitment channels discoverable and reducing impersonation-related confusion.

---

# 5. Proposed Product Experience

The product should revolve around one simple user action:

**"Verify this job opportunity for me."**

The investigation should require minimal effort from the user.

## Stage 1 — Opportunity submission

The user supplies any available information relating to the opportunity.

Supported forms could include:

- A job-posting URL.
- A copied email or recruiting message.
- A LinkedIn job listing.
- A recruiter email address.
- An application website.
- An offer letter or recruitment document.
- A screenshot containing relevant recruiting information.

The user should not need to understand technical indicators of fraud or manually investigate the employer beforehand.

The product begins by identifying the company, position, recruiter claims, application destination, and other relevant details.

If essential information is absent, it can ask the user for the missing details.

**User outcome:** The candidate can start an investigation from the information they already have.

## Stage 2 — Independent employer verification

The product attempts to establish whether the named employer is a legitimate, identifiable organization.

This includes examining authoritative company information and finding its independently established public presence.

The product must distinguish between:

- A confirmed organization.
- An organization with insufficient independent evidence.
- Conflicting claims regarding the employer's identity.
- An apparent impersonation of another organization.

An employer's existence alone must never be presented as proof that an offer or recruiter is authentic.

**User outcome:** The candidate understands whether the supposed employer can be independently identified.

## Stage 3 — Job opportunity verification

The product investigates whether the advertised vacancy corresponds to an opportunity published or otherwise acknowledged through a credible employer-controlled channel.

It compares relevant details, such as:

- Position title.
- Location and remote-work arrangement.
- Employment type.
- Responsibilities and qualifications.
- Compensation information, where publicly disclosed.
- Job or requisition identifiers.
- Application availability.

The product should recognize that job titles may differ slightly between platforms and that some valid opportunities are not publicly advertised.

Possible findings include:

**Officially confirmed:** A matching vacancy was independently located through an employer-recognized source.

**Partially matched:** Relevant evidence exists, but important details do not align or cannot be independently confirmed.

**Not independently located:** The product could not establish the existence of a corresponding public vacancy.

**Conflicting information:** Important advertised details contradict information found through a more authoritative source.

**User outcome:** The candidate learns whether the opportunity itself can be substantiated, without confusing an unsuccessful search with proof of fraud.

## Stage 4 — Recruiter and communication verification

The product examines whether the individual or organization contacting the candidate appears authorized to represent the employer.

Potential indicators include:

- Consistency between the claimed employer and sender domain.
- Independently recognizable recruiting-agency affiliations.
- Evidence of authorized recruitment partnerships.
- Conflicting contact or identity claims.
- Requests to communicate through unusual or unverifiable channels.

A different email domain must not automatically result in a fraud conclusion.

Some companies use third-party agencies, outsourced HR teams, or alternative official communication channels.

If an affiliation cannot be authenticated, the correct result is **unverified**, not automatically fraudulent.

**User outcome:** The candidate can distinguish a legitimate-looking vacancy from a verified recruitment relationship.

## Stage 5 — Application channel verification

The product independently identifies legitimate application destinations associated with the employer and vacancy.

It compares the link supplied by the recruiter against those destinations.

For example, a recruiter might supply a lookalike website while the company actually accepts applications through its official careers page.

Where the legitimate opportunity is found, the product should guide the user to the independently established application route.

If only a general employer careers page can be verified, the product must state that the exact role or application destination remains unconfirmed.

**User outcome:** The candidate is not left with a warning alone; they receive a practical and safer way to continue whenever one is available.

## Stage 6 — Evidence-backed investigation report

At the end of the investigation, the product presents a clear summary.

The report should answer four essential questions:

**What could be verified?**  
Facts supported by credible, identifiable sources.

**What could not be verified?**  
Recruiter claims, job details, or relationships for which sufficient evidence was unavailable.

**What appears suspicious or inconsistent?**  
Specific discrepancies, misleading information, or potentially harmful requests.

**What should the candidate do next?**  
A practical recommendation, such as continuing through an official application page, contacting the employer independently, requesting further information, or avoiding the supplied recruitment channel.

The report should not hide uncertainty behind an unexplained numerical trust score.

## Stage 7 — Resolution and follow-up

The product should guide candidates toward a clear next action rather than treating a generated report as the final objective.

Examples include:

- Continue through an independently verified official application destination.
- Verify a recruiter's affiliation through an employer-controlled contact channel.
- Request missing employment information before proceeding.
- Avoid sending payment or sensitive documents through an unverified channel.
- Save the investigation for later review.
- Recheck the opportunity when additional evidence becomes available.

For unclear cases, the product can prepare an appropriate verification request for the candidate to review and send.

Over time, the product could maintain a history of relevant communication and update findings as the situation develops.

**The desired outcome is informed action, not just information.**

---

# 6. Detailed Real-World Use Cases

## Use Case 1 — A fake recruiter impersonates a legitimate company

**Scenario**

A candidate receives an unsolicited message claiming to represent a recognizable technology company.

The message advertises an attractive position and includes an external application link.

The company's name, logo, and job description appear convincing.

**What the candidate needs**

To know whether the recruiter represents the company and whether the supplied application channel can be trusted.

**How the product helps**

The product independently identifies the company's official presence, searches for the advertised opportunity, and compares the supplied communication and application destination against credible hiring information.

It may find that the advertised job exists but the supplied application domain is unrelated to known employer channels.

**Expected outcome**

The product explains that the vacancy may be genuine while the recruiting approach remains unauthenticated.

If an official application destination is available, the candidate can proceed through it instead.

**Value delivered**

Avoids potentially unsafe application channels without unnecessarily discouraging the candidate from pursuing a legitimate position.

## Use Case 2 — A legitimate recruiter works for an external staffing agency

**Scenario**

A candidate receives a job offer from a recruiter using a staffing agency's email address.

The recruiter is not employed directly by the company offering the position.

A basic domain checker flags the message because the email does not match the employer's website.

**What the candidate needs**

To establish whether the different domain reflects an authorized recruitment arrangement rather than impersonation.

**How the product helps**

The product investigates the staffing firm's legitimacy, available recruitment relationships, the vacancy itself, and any employer-controlled evidence identifying approved recruiting partners.

It explicitly distinguishes organizational legitimacy from verified authorization to recruit for a particular job.

**Expected outcome**

If sufficient evidence is available, the product explains the relationship and identifies a safe way to proceed.

If the recruitment authorization cannot be established, it recommends independent employer confirmation rather than immediately labeling the recruiter fraudulent.

**Value delivered**

Reduces unnecessary false alarms and preserves legitimate opportunities.

## Use Case 3 — A genuine company is used to advertise a nonexistent vacancy

**Scenario**

A candidate sees a job listing for a real company, but the position cannot be found through any accessible official hiring channel.

The listing redirects candidates to an unrelated website.

**What the candidate needs**

To determine whether the role is real, outdated, unpublished, or potentially fabricated.

**How the product helps**

The product examines the company's known careers information, compares relevant postings, and investigates whether the role has an identifiable official source.

It assesses suspicious redirection separately from the absence of a public posting.

**Expected outcome**

The product identifies the unsupported claims and advises the candidate to seek confirmation through the employer's independent contact channels.

It does not classify the vacancy as fraudulent solely because it cannot find it.

**Value delivered**

Helps candidates avoid wasting time or disclosing information while respecting the possibility of legitimate unadvertised roles.

## Use Case 4 — A recruiter requests money before onboarding

**Scenario**

A candidate is informed that they passed an interview and must pay an equipment deposit, registration charge, or verification fee before receiving a contract.

The message emphasizes urgency.

**What the candidate needs**

To understand the risk and know what to do before transferring money.

**How the product helps**

The product identifies the financial request, examines the communication for coercive or inconsistent claims, and checks for independently verifiable employer instructions.

It clearly separates suspicious conduct from facts that have been authenticated.

**Expected outcome**

The candidate receives a prominent recommendation not to transfer money through an unverified process, alongside an independently established contact route for further confirmation where available.

**Value delivered**

Helps prevent financial losses at a particularly vulnerable point in the recruitment process.

## Use Case 5 — A candidate is asked to upload sensitive personal documents

**Scenario**

A supposed recruiter asks for government identity documents, bank details, or other sensitive information before a formal recruitment relationship can be established.

The candidate is unsure whether the request is part of normal onboarding.

**What the candidate needs**

To understand whether the request is consistent with a verified recruitment process and which aspects require further confirmation.

**How the product helps**

The product investigates the recruitment source, timing of the request, stated purpose, and application destination.

It explains the uncertainty and recommends verifying the recipient and process independently.

**Expected outcome**

The candidate avoids prematurely sharing sensitive information through an unverified channel.

**Value delivered**

Reduces unnecessary exposure to identity misuse and personal-data theft.

## Use Case 6 — A job offer has conflicting employment information

**Scenario**

A candidate receives an offer describing a remote position with a particular salary, but the company's official listing describes a different location, employment type, or compensation range.

**What the candidate needs**

To understand whether the differences are normal negotiation changes, stale information, a separate role, or suspicious inconsistencies.

**How the product helps**

The product compares the recruitment details against independently established sources and identifies material differences.

It explains which changes may legitimately occur during hiring and which require employer confirmation.

**Expected outcome**

The candidate receives specific questions to clarify before proceeding.

**Value delivered**

Supports better employment decisions without treating every discrepancy as fraud.

## Use Case 7 — The candidate receives several messages about the same opportunity

**Scenario**

A candidate initially receives an opportunity through LinkedIn, later receives an email, and is eventually redirected to another application website.

The claims change across these conversations.

**What the candidate needs**

A consolidated understanding of the opportunity rather than repeatedly checking individual messages.

**How the product helps**

The product associates the messages with the same investigation, compares claims across stages, identifies newly introduced inconsistencies, and revises its assessment when credible evidence changes.

**Expected outcome**

The candidate understands what changed, whether earlier verification still applies, and which next actions remain appropriate.

**Value delivered**

Provides continuity and reduces the burden of monitoring a developing recruitment process.

**Product scope:** This is a subsequent capability rather than a requirement for the initial release.

---

# 7. How Results Should Be Communicated

A major product differentiator should be the clarity and honesty of its findings.

A single score such as "92% legitimate" risks creating a false impression of certainty.

Instead, each investigation should provide an evidence-based assessment across distinct dimensions.

| Investigation dimension | Example result |
|---|---|
| Employer identity | Independently confirmed |
| Advertised vacancy | Matching official posting found |
| Recruiter affiliation | Could not be verified |
| Supplied application link | Does not match established hiring channel |
| Requests for payment | Suspicious request detected |
| Official application destination | Independently confirmed |

The overall guidance should use carefully defined outcomes:

### Verified route available

An authentic application destination has been independently established.

This does not guarantee that any external recruiter's claims or the eventual employment terms are authentic.

### Further verification required

Some information is credible, but a critical part of the recruitment interaction cannot yet be authenticated.

### Significant warning indicators

The available evidence identifies material concerns, such as a misleading destination, impersonation indicators, or an unexpected payment request.

### Insufficient evidence

The product cannot reliably establish the opportunity's authenticity.

It should explain what evidence is missing and how the candidate may obtain it safely.

This approach makes the product trustworthy by acknowledging the boundaries of what it knows.

---

# 8. What Makes the Product Different?

## 8.1 It investigates rather than simply classifies

Traditional scam detection can focus on suspicious keywords, domains, and known fraudulent patterns.

Our product looks at the full recruitment claim and gathers independent supporting evidence.

## 8.2 It separates employer, vacancy, recruiter, and application authenticity

These are different questions.

A company can be legitimate while a recruiter impersonates it. A vacancy can be real while an application website is fraudulent.

The product evaluates each separately.

## 8.3 It prioritizes safe continuation

The goal is not merely to discourage suspicious opportunities.

Where possible, it helps candidates locate the actual position and continue through an independently verified channel.

## 8.4 It handles ambiguous recruitment practices

Legitimate external agencies, confidential vacancies, expired listings, and unusual employer communications can all create uncertainty.

The product must account for these situations instead of making simplistic assumptions.

## 8.5 It provides evidence users can examine

Every important conclusion should be accompanied by an explanation and relevant source information.

Candidates should be able to understand why a warning was raised or a destination was recommended.

## 8.6 It can remain useful throughout a recruitment journey

The longer-term vision is to reassess a saved opportunity when new communication, documentation, or other evidence appears.

This transforms verification from a one-time lookup into an ongoing decision-support service.

---

# 9. Initial Product Scope

The first version should solve one problem extremely well:

**Help a candidate investigate a recruiting opportunity and identify the safest supported way to continue.**

### Essential capabilities

1. Accept a job listing, application link, or recruiting message.
2. Identify the organization and employment opportunity.
3. Independently establish the employer's credible public presence.
4. Attempt to locate a matching official vacancy.
5. Examine the recruitment channel and supplied application destination.
6. Identify material discrepancies and warning signals.
7. Produce an understandable report with evidence and uncertainty.
8. Present an independently verified application route when available.
9. Recommend concrete next steps when the investigation remains unresolved.

### Not included in the initial product

- Automatically submitting job applications.
- Guaranteed identification of every fraudulent recruiter.
- Background checks on private individuals.
- Automatic contact with recruiters without user approval.
- Uploading personal documents to external applications.
- Providing immigration, employment-law, or financial guarantees.
- Making claims that an offer is completely safe or that employment is guaranteed.
- Acting as a job board or replacing established recruitment services.

These exclusions allow the product to concentrate on a valuable, realistic, and trustworthy initial experience.

---

# 10. Intended User Journey

### Step 1 — Discovery

The candidate receives or finds an employment opportunity and feels uncertain about its legitimacy.

### Step 2 — Submission

They open the product and paste the relevant link or message.

### Step 3 — Investigation

The product independently examines the employer, advertised vacancy, recruiter claims, and application destination.

### Step 4 — Explanation

The candidate receives a structured assessment distinguishing confirmed facts, unresolved claims, discrepancies, and warning indicators.

### Step 5 — Recommended action

The product presents the most appropriate next action based on available evidence.

### Step 6 — Outcome

The candidate either continues through an independently established hiring route, requests verification through a credible channel, or avoids an opportunity presenting serious unresolved concerns.

### Step 7 — Optional follow-up

The candidate can save the case and provide additional information later, allowing the assessment to be updated.

**The experience should feel like receiving help from a careful, independent investigator—not interacting with a generic chatbot.**

---

# 11. Expected Product Value

## For individual candidates

**Confidence:** Better understanding of what is verified and what remains uncertain.

**Protection:** Reduced exposure to suspicious payment requests, impersonation, and unsafe data collection.

**Efficiency:** Less manual effort searching company websites and comparing job postings.

**Opportunity preservation:** A better chance of finding the genuine application route when a suspicious message references a real vacancy.

**Clarity:** Specific next steps instead of vague warnings.

## For educational institutions

**Student protection:** A practical tool for evaluating unfamiliar internships and graduate recruitment opportunities.

**Scalable support:** A consistent verification experience available to many students.

**Career awareness:** Greater understanding of recruitment safety and appropriate verification practices.

## For employers and recruitment platforms

**Brand protection:** Potential to help candidates identify legitimate employer-controlled recruitment destinations.

**Trust:** Better visibility into recognized hiring channels.

**Candidate safety:** Reduced opportunities for impersonators to redirect candidates away from genuine recruitment processes.

---

# 12. Product Success Criteria

The product should not be assessed only by the number of opportunities scanned.

Its success depends on whether it helps users make safer, better-informed decisions.

| Objective | How success can be evaluated |
|---|---|
| Verify authentic opportunities | Proportion of supported genuine opportunities correctly matched to authoritative sources |
| Avoid harmful recommendations | Frequency of unsafe links incorrectly recommended as legitimate |
| Minimize false accusations | Rate at which legitimate opportunities are incorrectly described as fraudulent |
| Provide useful outcomes | Percentage of investigations that return a verified next step or a clear reason verification remains impossible |
| Establish user confidence | Whether users understand the evidence and feel able to make an informed decision |
| Reduce manual effort | Time and number of steps saved compared with independent verification |
| Support continued engagement | Whether users return with new opportunities or follow-up evidence |
| Support commercial adoption | Institutional trials, repeat usage, paid conversion, and customer retention |

A successful investigation does not always end with an official application link.

Sometimes, the correct outcome is identifying insufficient evidence and helping the candidate avoid an unsupported assumption.

This must be recognized as a valid and useful result.

---

# 13. SaaS Business Opportunity

The product has potential across both consumer and institutional segments.

## Consumer offering

A free or low-cost service allowing candidates to investigate individual opportunities.

Possible paid benefits could include additional investigations, saved case histories, reassessments, and ongoing recruitment monitoring.

However, individual job searching is often temporary, which may limit subscription duration.

## Educational institutions

Universities, training organizations, and career centers could provide the service to students as part of their career-support resources.

This offers a possible recurring business model with broader distribution.

Individual investigation details should remain private unless the student explicitly authorizes sharing.

## Recruitment platforms

Job platforms and career services could incorporate verification capabilities into their existing candidate experiences.

This would require additional partnerships, product validation, and careful consideration of accuracy and liability.

## Employer participation

In the longer term, employers could help candidates identify recognized recruiting partners and official application channels.

This could improve the quality of verification evidence, but it depends on employer participation and cannot be assumed during initial launch.

**The initial commercialization hypothesis should prioritize user adoption and evidence of genuine utility, followed by testing institutional and platform-based revenue models.**

---

# 14. Future Product Expansion

The initial product should remain focused, but several natural opportunities exist.

### Phase 1 — Independent opportunity verification

Candidates submit recruitment information and receive evidence-backed findings and a safe next action.

### Phase 2 — Ongoing recruitment case assistance

Candidates can maintain a history of messages, offer changes, and newly received documents relating to the same opportunity.

The product identifies material changes and recommends further checks.

### Phase 3 — Candidate-side employment safety workspace

Users can manage multiple ongoing investigations and receive relevant updates about previously assessed opportunities.

### Phase 4 — Institutional verification services

Universities and recruitment platforms can provide verification access to larger groups.

### Phase 5 — Employer-recognized recruitment channels

Participating employers can publish or confirm recognized hiring domains and authorized recruitment channels.

The product can use this information to improve the strength and transparency of its assessments.

These phases are possible directions, not commitments or proof of market demand.

---

# 15. Product Principles and Trust Boundaries

The value of this service depends on users trusting its conclusions.

That trust must be earned through accurate evidence, transparent reasoning, and clear boundaries.

**Evidence before conclusions:** Important findings must be supported by identifiable sources.

**Uncertainty must remain visible:** Missing evidence cannot automatically be treated as evidence of fraud.

**No absolute safety promises:** Even an authentic application channel cannot guarantee a fair, safe, or legitimate eventual employment arrangement.

**Candidate control:** Users decide whether to apply, contact an employer, share documents, or take any consequential action.

**Privacy by default:** Sensitive recruitment messages and personal data should not be exposed or shared unnecessarily.

**Independent verification:** Information supplied by a potentially suspicious recruiter should not be the sole basis for verifying that same recruiter.

**No discriminatory assessments:** The product evaluates verifiable recruitment claims and behaviors, not assumptions based on names, nationalities, identities, or protected characteristics.

**Explainable recommendations:** Users should understand what was found, what remains unresolved, and why a particular next step is recommended.

**Respect legitimate recruitment diversity:** External recruiters, nonpublic vacancies, and nonstandard hiring arrangements are not inherently fraudulent.

---

# 16. Final Product Narrative

The modern job market offers candidates more opportunities than ever, but also exposes them to increasingly convincing recruitment impersonation and misleading application channels.

Candidates often lack the resources, experience, or time required to independently investigate every opportunity they encounter.

Existing safety measures frequently focus on warning indicators without helping candidates determine what is genuinely verifiable or how to continue safely.

**Our product addresses that gap by acting as an independent employment-opportunity investigation and navigation assistant.**

Given a recruitment message or job listing, it establishes what can be verified about the employer, advertised position, recruiting relationship, and application destination.

It identifies meaningful inconsistencies, explains uncertainty, and helps candidates reach legitimate hiring channels whenever sufficient evidence is available.

For suspicious or unresolved opportunities, it guides candidates toward safer verification actions instead of making unsupported promises.

The initial product focuses on one measurable outcome:

**Turning an uncertain recruitment opportunity into an evidence-backed decision with a practical, safer next step.**

Over time, this can evolve into a broader employment-trust service for individuals, educational institutions, job platforms, and employers.

The long-term ambition is to make independently verifiable recruitment information accessible to everyone—not only candidates with established professional networks or recruitment expertise.

**Core value proposition:** *Know who is actually hiring, understand what you can trust, and find a safer way to apply.*

I've folded your vision and the research into a sharper concept, and three agents are now building in parallel. Nothing is pushed yet.

**How I sharpened the idea** (the full brief is `artifacts/locke-1/concept-brief.md`):
- **Positioning:** "Locke: know who's really hiring. Evidence before trust." The name nods to John Locke, the philosopher who held that knowledge comes from evidence, plus a lock for safety.
- **Agent design:** the hackathon wants one agent that finishes a substantial task end to end, so Locke runs as a pipeline:
  - it extracts the claims from what you paste, and asks a follow-up question if something essential is missing;
  - a planner decides which checks to run;
  - five checks run in parallel (employer, vacancy, recruiter, application link, risky requests);
  - a skeptic step challenges every finding to stop false accusations;
  - a final step picks the verdict and the verified apply link, or drafts a verification email for you to send yourself.
- **Real evidence sources:** the public job-board APIs of Greenhouse, Lever and Ashby, Crustdata (a sponsor) for company data, domain registration age and email DNS records, and lookalike-domain detection.
- **Built-in recovery demo:** if a careers page can't be read, it falls back to the job-board API, then to web search. If all fail, the vacancy is marked "not independently located", never "fraud".
- **Before/after numbers:** a set of about 25 labelled cases, scored on accuracy, false-accusation rate, and how often an unsafe link gets recommended (that one has to be 0). We run it, fix failures using the neatlogs traces, and run it again. The per-run cost neatlogs measures feeds the cfo.ai business plan, which ties all three required tools together.
- **Five pages:** landing, investigate, a live case view ending in the report, a public scoreboard of the before/after results, and a methodology page.

**Agents running:**

| Session | Agent | Task |
|---|---|---|
| `ao://sessions/locke/locke-4` | Claude Code | `AGENTS.md` (the rulebook every agent follows, including how work is split between them), `CLAUDE.md` (which skills to use when), `docs/SPEC.md`, `docs/PLAN.md` (time-boxed tasks across all 4 agents), `hackathon.md`, `.env.example` |

Cursor gets the product UI as soon as the spec and brand land. Then Codex takes the evidence-gathering tools and Claude Code the agent itself.

**The stack is all TypeScript, no Python.** neatlogs has a native TypeScript SDK that traces LangGraph runs directly. The main risk is that it's documented against an older version of the LangChain libraries. So we pin those versions, and the first gate is proving that one run appears in neatlogs before anything else gets built.

+- **No extra infrastructure, and it's already next to your data.** The gateway lives inside your Neon project (and is injected into Neon Functions automatically), runs on the same Databricks infrastructure that serves trillions of tokens a month, and supports streaming (SSE) out of the box.
+| `NEON_AI_GATEWAY_TOKEN`    | Gateway bearer token (a Neon credential, `nt_live_...`)                                                                              |
+> Neon injects **only** these two vars — it does **not** set `OPENAI_API_KEY` / `OPENAI_BASE_URL`. The `@neon/ai-sdk-provider` and Mastra's `neon/<model>` read `NEON_AI_GATEWAY_*` directly (zero config); for the plain OpenAI SDK / `@ai-sdk/openai`, build the client's `apiKey` + `baseURL` from them (shown below), or set your own `OPENAI_*` by hand (`env pull` leaves user-set vars untouched).
+For typed, validated access to the injected credentials, pass the same `neon.ts` config object to `parseEnv` from `@neon/env` — it returns an `env.aiGateway` namespace (`apiKey`, `baseUrl`) derived from your config.
+The dedicated `@neon/ai-sdk-provider` reads `NEON_AI_GATEWAY_BASE_URL` + `NEON_AI_GATEWAY_TOKEN` from the injected env with **zero config** and routes each model to the best endpoint (Anthropic → Messages, OpenAI/Codex → Responses, everything else → MLflow). On a Neon Function that streams text and generates images, just pick a catalog model:
+> Prefer `@neon/ai-sdk-provider` over the bare `@ai-sdk/openai` `openai()`: Neon injects only `NEON_AI_GATEWAY_*`, not `OPENAI_*`, so `openai()` won't pick up the gateway from the env on its own. If you do use `@ai-sdk/openai`, configure it explicitly with `createOpenAI({ apiKey: process.env.NEON_AI_GATEWAY_TOKEN, baseURL: `${process.env.NEON_AI_GATEWAY_BASE_URL}/openai/v1` })`.
+[Mastra](https://mastra.ai) is the recommended framework when you want batteries-included agents — built-in memory, tools, workflows, and tracing — with the model still pointed at the gateway. With `@mastra/core` 1.47+, use a `neon/<model>` magic string; Mastra reads `NEON_AI_GATEWAY_BASE_URL` and `NEON_AI_GATEWAY_TOKEN` from the environment (injected by `neon deploy` when `aiGateway` is enabled). Use `parseEnv` only for other declared services (e.g. `env.postgres.databaseUrl` for `@mastra/pg` memory):
+When you don't need an agent framework — a single completion, an existing provider-SDK integration, or native provider features — call the gateway with the plain SDKs. Neon injects the `NEON_AI_GATEWAY_*` vars (not `OPENAI_*`), so set the client's `apiKey` + `baseURL` from them. For the OpenAI **Responses** dialect (`/openai/v1`):

+  apiKey: process.env.NEON_AI_GATEWAY_TOKEN,
